content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper argues based on prior work that the encoding of positional information from padding, abbreviated PPP by convolutional neural networks is an undesired property that can have unwanted side-effects. The degree to which PPP is learned as a consequence of different padding techniques is investigated and a new way to quantify it is proposed. In addition a new padding technique is explored, which could help to lower PPP.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---------
- Investigating PPP makes sense and the method proposed to do this is relatively simple.

- The experiments are thorough and relatively large in scale showing clear results.

- An ability to reliably quantify PPP is a requirement for further understanding of its consequences and possibly ways of mitigating its effects.

Weaknesses
----------
- Some table and figure captions are lacking details and/or are confusing.
  - Figure 1 is placed and referenced so early in the manuscript that it is hard to understand what it contains. E.g. what is the sampling process, how are the two signals generated, how is PP quantified? What is the right column in relation to the other four?
  - I suggest you explain what the numbers indicate in table 1. Also this is a very large table with a lot of information that is only referenced once in text and in a single short sentence. Is all of this information really necessary?
  - Table 2 is also relatively large, and I find it hard to deduce from the text what numbers should be compared and how this relates to the title in bold. Consider helping the reader a bit more.
  - Table 3, here the caption seems a bit misleading. "The results show a consistent and significant increment of PPP is developed through the model training". Somehow this seems more fitting as a description of Figure 5, as table 3 seems to be about pretraining and it only compares pretraining with no pretraining.

- As far as I understand Table 2 it shows the different possitional encoding measurement metrics (SPC, MAE, and PPP-MAE) for the different padding schemes and models. In section 4.2 it is concluded that because the standard deviations are larger than the differences between the padding variants, the PosENet based metrics cannot be used to say much about the benefits of these padding methods. While this may be true, as far as I can deduce, this does not necessarily indicate a problem with the PosENet based metrics, it may also just be the case that PPP varies a lot over training runs.

- An intuitive explanation for the equations given (1, 2, and 3) would help understanding.

 Other smaller annoyances
  - Consider avoiding the abbreviation of method names in the abstract or write what they are.
  - "Padding, one of the most fundamental components in neural network architectures, has received much less attention than other modules in the literature", what do you mean by this? What is a module in this context?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- On clarity, despite the simplicity of the equations and the experiments conducted, I find the work relatively hard to read. More details is given under weaknesses.

- On quality, despite its clarity issues, I like the work. The manuscript could be improved if the method was used to propose a padding technique that actually made a difference in terms of the investigated metrics.

- On novelty, I don't find it particularly surprising that neural networks can and do learn to detect padded values in order to inform about locations. I also think the idea that the proposed randn padding scheme would alleviate this to be a long shot. It seems to me that in order to really be able to really match the distribution in the padded regions more advanced techniques are needed. One could imagine using adversarial learning or other methods for generating realistic image data. Despite this, the work is looking at a previously largely overlooked aspect of neural network architecture design choice and making meaningful contributions to quantifying how well these choices work.

- On reproducibility, code and data collection scripts will be made available on acceptance, which would make it easier to reproduce.

content.title: Thanks for the review. Here are our responses.
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the comprehensive review. Here, we discuss the raised weaknesses and questions:

1. **`Some table and figure captions are lacking details and/or are confusing.`**

    We thank the reviewer for the suggestions and will fix the mentioned figure captions. 
    - For Table 1, despite only the zeros-padding being needed, we present the table similar to the F-Conv paper, in case readers suspect we cherrypick certain paddings. We will reduce the size of the table and move the whole table to Appendix.
    - For Table 2, the colors are designed to help readers find that all numbers produced by PosENet are not meaningful with the high deviation. We will add the following note to its caption: “Notice that the majority of the PosENet numbers are being marked orange, which shows the deviation of PosENet is too high considering the numerical differences among padding schemes.”
    - For Table 3, the captions were describing the contrast between the random initialized networks versus the pretrained networks. We will change the wording from `developed through the model training` to `developed *after* the model training`.
    - For Figure 1, we will move it a few pages back to the methodology section, and add more discussions to the visualization in the same section. The number of samples labeled in the figure is marking the number of samples from the evaluation dataset, for instance, the GMap dataset we used in the paper. The left-four column shows the feature map visualization, and the rightmost column shows the clean extraction of PPP with our formulation. The figure aims to illustrate how PPP is inspired and achieves a clean extraction from the noisy features.

2. **`It may also just be the case that PPP varies a lot over training runs.`**

    Given the context, we assume the reviewer is actually referring PosENet in this question. If that is the case, we should observe a similar level of variance reflected in PPP metrics, but in reality, PPP shows a very low deviation over the models using the same architecture-padding setting. Also, despite not being shown, we observe a similar level of variance even if we measure PosENet on the exact same model multiple times, the high variance is purely caused by PosENet convergence. Besides, we practically observe that the shape of PPP is not only consistent across models using the same padding scheme. In Figures 7, 8, and 9, the patterns are even sharing some similarities among different padding schemes.

3. **`Padding, one of the most fundamental components in neural network architectures, has received much less attention than other modules in the literature", what do you mean by this? What is a module in this context?`**

    By module, we refer to everything else, for instance, the architecture, optimizers, regularizations, and losses. Despite nearly completely not being attended, padding itself is a standalone module, it can be swapped without changing the course of the remaining architectural designs of a neural network.

4. **`One could imagine using adversarial learning or other methods for generating realistic image data.`**

    We have considered this approach at the early stage of the project. However, the computational costs are too high for paddings, which are being used throughout the network, and require to be efficient for both training and inference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the Position-information Pattern from Padding (PPP) encoded in neural networks. PPP is defined as difference between algorithmically and optimally padded activations, then SNR and MAE are computed on the difference to quantify how much PPP exists. The result shows a pre-trained CNN model contains a lot of position information. Comparing with the two previous studies, this paper is claimed to be more robust and reliable for PPP evaluation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: This study investigates a fundamental question that affects all convolutional neural networks used in computer vision. The proposed method seems to have lower variability than the other methods.

Weaknesses:
This study did not discuss how the PPP affects CNNs in practice. The proposed padding did not compare against other commonly used paddings in vision application to show its efficacy, which is not convincing. The padding scheme designed in Section 2.4 is to weaken PPP detected by eq3, which is based on an optimal padding solution as shown in eq2. It is better to discuss why cropping from a bigger picture can be considered a theoretical optimal padding. Having more content(pixels) could (slightly)deliver more semantic information, but I do not think the information can be associated with PPP, and the proposed padding is also algorithmical solution.

content.title: Thanks for the review. Here are our responses.
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the comprehensive review. Here, we discuss the raised weaknesses and questions:

1. **`This study did not discuss how the PPP affects CNNs in practice.`**

     The negative side effects caused by the positional information have been well-studied in the existing work cited in our manuscript. Especially, Islam et al [A], Alsallakh et al [B], and Innamorati et al [C] studied the pratical issues of PPP in CNN applications.

     - [A] Md Amirul Islam, Matthew Kowal, Sen Jia, Konstantinos G. Derpanis, and Neil Bruce. Boundary effects in {cnn}s: Feature or bug? https://openreview.net/forum?id=M4qXqdw3xC, 2021a.
     - [B] Bilal Alsallakh, Narine Kokhlikyan, Vivek Miglani, Jun Yuan, and Orion Reblitz-Richardson. Mind the pad – {cnn}s can develop blind spots. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021a.
     - [C] Carlo Innamorati, Tobias Ritschel, Tim Weyrich, and Niloy J Mitra. Learning on the edge: Investigating boundary filters in cnns. International Journal of Computer Vision, 2020.

2. **`The proposed padding did not compare against other commonly used paddings in vision application to show its efficacy, which is not convincing.`**

    In Table 2, we perform a comprehensive comparison between the proposed Randn padding versus most of the commonly used padding schemes. The purpose of Randn is to show that PPP is not purely created 

3. **`The padding scheme designed in Section 2.4 is to weaken PPP detected by eq3, which is based on an optimal padding solution as shown in eq2.`**

    The proposed Randn padding scheme is an effort of adding randomness to the padding scheme. It is not directly associated with optimal padding. 

4. **`It is better to discuss why cropping from a bigger picture can be considered a theoretical optimal padding. Having more content(pixels) could (slightly)deliver more semantic information, but I do not think the information can be associated with PPP, and the proposed padding is also algorithmical solution.`***

    We provide the following anonymized link to a figure to illustrate why the optimal padding is deemed to be optimal: https://imgur.com/a/bGaeBnd

    We illustrate Eq 1 and Eq 2 with a simple 3-layer CNN with 3x3 convolutional kernels. Note that the real model with downsampling will significantly reinforce the severity of the issue.

    - **(Left)** We mark the padding pixels in red with algorithmic padding schemes, mark the receptive fields affected by the padding information in pink, then mark the feature values affected by the padding information in orange. 

    - **(Right)** In contrast, for optimal padding, we calculate the required input padding (illustrated in Eq 2, and calculated the feature sizes in Appendix A). For instance, in this example, we pad the input with three pixels, OA1, OA2, and OA3. Then, we no longer need padding pixels in the following layers, the features are purely based on the inputs (OB1 is produced by OA1-OA3). We mark the pixels made available due to the optimal padding in blue. The same set of orange pixels is now supported with optimally padded information (OA1-OA3), instead of the red padding pixels.

    Back to the question, with correct calculation, OA1-OA3 provides the exact real-world information that is replaced with the algorithmic padding. It is exactly describing the optimal features a neural network should produce if no padding is introduced/needed. Therefore, you can notice that there is no padding in the right part of the figure.

    Randn padding still pads the features, and the padding pixels affect its surrounding pixels, causing complicated interactions and leading to the final PPP we visualized in Figure 7-9.

5. **`The proposed padding strategy is sampling from a normal distribution which is learned within a sliding window, its novelty is limited. More importantly, its efficacy has not been validated in practice comparing to other padding strategy.`**

    We do not claim its design novel, we use it as an important case study showing that stochasticity cannot avoid the construction of PPP. We study its efficacy in Table 2. Its performance is similar to other commonly used padding schemes, and it avoids PPP in VGG-19 architecture, but it does not fundamentally destruct PPP.

content.title: Thanks for the review. Here are our responses.
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the comprehensive review. Here, we discuss the raised weaknesses and questions:

1. **`PPP metrics are potentially biased by the model architecture and parameters.`**

     Our approach has avoided the randomness and biases from the convergence of optimization-based PosENet metric, which is significant progress considering the reliability of existing methods. However, the limitation pointed out by the review is an inevitable drawback as long as the evaluation uses the features extracted from a trained model, while the PPP is a training artifact learned by the model. This is the “chicken and egg” dilemma, PPP needs to be generated first before it can be quantified.

2. **`Only some basically networks were used in analysis so generalizability to more SOTA network architectures still needs exploration.`**

     In terms of SOTA, we assume it refers to transformer-based architectures. Transformers explicitly use absolute position encoding within their architecture. However, several recent efforts [1,2] bring convolutional layers back to the architecture, which still inherently suffers from the similar PPP artifacts studied in our work.

    - [1] “A ConvNet for the 2020s”
    - [2] “CoAtNet: Marrying Convolution and Attention for All Data Sizes”

3. **`I wonder if the authors can illustrate some of undesired effects of padding on certain real world examples in addition to just showing the edge view of those blue-yellow blocks.`**

     We would suggest some great visualizations provided in previous papers, as they have brought many great illustrations of the problem with real data.
      - Figure 1 in “Mind the Pad -- CNNs can Develop Blind Spots”
      - Figure 14 in “Boundary Effects in CNNs: Feature or Bug?”

display_title: Thanks for the review. Here are our responses.

content.title: Thanks for the review. Here are our responses.
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the comprehensive review. The raised questions mainly focus on two perspectives: (a) the importance/value of the negative effects caused by PPP, and (b) how the proposed metrics help to address the issue.

1. **`The importance/value of the negative effects caused by PPP`**

    The negative side effects caused by the positional information have been well-supported/proven by several previous papers cited in our manuscript (the first paragraph of section 1, and the last paragraph of section 1). We will increase the discussion of these previous discoveries in the next revision, please allow us to elaborate on the issues here descriptively.

    > Islam et al [1] first demonstrate CNN models encode positional information. Soon in the subsequent study [2], Islam et al. show that positional information alters the model prediction by the object's location. In addition, Alsallakh et al. [3] show that padding crippled the object detection performance in practice, while Innamorati et al. [4] study such a prediction error on the edge of the feature map. The positional information is also being shown harmful in other tasks, such as time-series prediction [5] and differentiable equation modeling [6]. Recent research [7,8,9,10] in the generative modeling community also discovers positional information needs to be removed or carefully re-designed in certain synthesis tasks. 

    > These critical pieces of evidence all are pointing out that the existing positional information from padding is an ill-designed component and causes many undesired side effects. Our study further reveals the issue with carefully designed metrics with proper definitions, facilitating future studies on correctly quantifying the effectiveness of remedies. These existing studies (including ours) only reveal the tip of the iceberg. Future studies on real-world vision-driven products are needed, which is beyond the scope and resources available for academic research.

     - [1] Md Amirul Islam*, Sen Jia*, and Neil D. B. Bruce. How much position information do convolutional neural networks encode? In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020.
     - [2] Md Amirul Islam, Matthew Kowal, Sen Jia, Konstantinos G. Derpanis, and Neil Bruce. Boundary effects in {cnn}s: Feature or bug? https://openreview.net/forum?id=M4qXqdw3xC, 2021a.
     - [3] Bilal Alsallakh, Narine Kokhlikyan, Vivek Miglani, Jun Yuan, and Orion Reblitz-Richardson. Mind the pad – {cnn}s can develop blind spots. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021a.
     - [4] Carlo Innamorati, Tobias Ritschel, Tim Weyrich, and Niloy J Mitra. Learning on the edge: Investigating boundary filters in cnns. International Journal of Computer Vision, 2020.
     - [5] Songwei Ge, Thomas Hayes, Harry Yang, Xi Yin, Guan Pang, David Jacobs, Jia-Bin Huang, and Devi Parikh. Long video generation with time-agnostic vqgan and time-sensitive transformer.
     - [6] Antonio Alguacil, Wagner Gonçalves Pinto, Michael Bauerheim, Marc C Jacob, and Stéphane Moreau. Effects of boundary conditions in fully convolutional networks for learning spatio-temporal dynamics. In Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases, 2021.
     - [7] Chieh Hubert Lin, Yen-Chi Cheng, Hsin-Ying Lee, Sergey Tulyakov, and Ming-Hsuan Yang. InfinityGAN: Towards infinite-pixel image synthesis. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022.
     - [8] Rui Xu, Xintao Wang, Kai Chen, Bolei Zhou, and Chen Change Loy. Positional encoding as spatial inductive bias in gans. In IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2021.
     - [9] Evangelos Ntavelis, Mohamad Shahbazi, Iason Kastanis, Radu Timofte, Martin Danelljan, and Luc Van Gool. Arbitrary-scale image synthesis. In IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2022.
     - [10] Jooyoung Choi, Jungbeom Lee, Yonghyun Jeong, and Sungroh Yoon. Toward spatially unbiased generative models. In IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision, 2021.

---

2. **`How the proposed metrics help to address the issue.`**

    Regarding resolving the problem, we may need to view the necessity of this paper from another perspective. To resolve a fundamental issue, the problem needs to be well-defined first, and the researchers urge a reliable metric to measure the existence of the problem and improvements while proposing solutions. We found there are no formal definitions of PPP, therefore the existing metrics remain empirical. This leads to (a) the unreliable metric PosENet in Section 3.1, and (b) the erroneous conclusions we show in Section 3.2. Our definitions, metrics, and analyses pave the way for future research toward fundamentally addressing the PPP-related issues.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for your response. 

> I think this work should directly have experiments with that generalization goal in order to demonstrate relevance.

I think this point is very important to resolve. One idea is to construct a scatterplot with the PPP-MAE score and generalization performance over multiple runs (and PosENet as well). And to have a plot like this for multiple datasets. Then it could be clear that PPP-MAE has a higher correlation with generalization than PosENet. 

I would also find it very convincing if there was a task that caused a catastrophic failure in generalization when positional information was encoded and this could be detected by PPP-MAE. Potentially a synthetic task where you can control how relevant the positional information is.

I think without some explicit generalization conclusions I think the contribution is not concrete enough.
